activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: In the song 'Five Little Monkeys Jumping on the Bed', one monkey falls off each time, so the number gets one smaller.
story:
Josephine loved the monkey song. But today the monkey toys were up high on the shelf. She could not reach them. "Can you help me?" she asked Miss Ana. "Yes, I can," said Miss Ana. She took down the five little monkeys and poured them into Josephine's lap. They tickled her hands.

Josephine lined them up on the rug. Five monkeys, side by side. She sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!" She made one monkey fall off. Bump. Now she saw four monkeys on the rug. She sang again, "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed!" Another monkey fell. Bump. Now there were three. Then two. Then one. Then none.

A boy named Sam watched. His face looked grumpy. "Where did the monkeys go?" he asked. "They fell off the bed," said Josephine. "Each one went bump." Sam sat down next to her. Together they counted one, two, three, four, five. All the monkeys came back to the rug.

Miss Ana clapped her hands. "Sing it one more time," she said. Josephine held the monkeys like a warm little nest in her hands. She counted them softly. "One, two, three, four, five." Then she lifted the first monkey high and began, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed..."

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: A book in English starts at the front cover, and you turn the pages until you reach the back.
story:
Milan went to the store with his dad. He wanted a book about trucks. He saw a bin of little books by the door. A blue book had a big truck on the front. Milan picked it up.

He sat down on the floor to look. He opened the book from the wrong side. The pages felt odd. The truck picture came at the end, not at the start. The story seemed all mixed up. Milan turned the book over. Now the truck was on the front cover. He opened it from the front. The first page showed a little red truck. Page by page, the truck drove to a big hill.

"Can we get this one?" Milan asked. Dad said, "Yes. Let's go fetch a basket." Milan held the blue book tight. It did not fall, not even once.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: At school, children take turns on the playground slide.
story:
Ava held her teacher's hand. It was her first day of school. Her shoes were pink. Her bag had bread inside for snack time. "Will you stay with me?" Ava asked. "I will stay close by," said Miss Kim.

Outside, Ava saw the big slide. She ran to it fast. A boy named Sam was at the front. He went down. Then he ran back to go again. But Miss Kim showed him the back of the line. Ava got in line behind two friends. She waited. She watched. Each friend went down, one at a time. Then it was her turn. Whee! Down she went, fast as a bird.

Ava ran to the back of the line again. Soon it was her turn one more time. "The line works," said Ava. Sam smiled and stood behind her. "My turn next," he said.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: On a tablet, you tap the screen with your finger to choose things.
story:
Beatrice sat on Grandma's big soft chair. Grandma's tablet lay on the table. It was dark and still.

Beatrice wanted to draw a ball on it. She pushed the screen with her whole hand. Nothing happened. The screen stayed dark. She pushed again, hard. Still nothing. "Hmm," said Beatrice. "How does it wake up?"

Grandma tapped the little button once. The screen lit up. "Now you try," said Grandma. Beatrice tapped the button with one finger. Click! The screen woke up. "It likes my finger," said Beatrice.

She saw the little paint pot picture. She tapped it once with one finger. The drawing app opened. Beatrice drew a big red ball. She drew a soft gray cat too.

Then she was done. She swept her finger over the screen and made a curvy sun. "All finished," she said. She gave the tablet to Grandma. Grandma put it away in the drawer, safe and snug.

"More drawing tomorrow?" asked Grandma. Beatrice nodded. "Yes! With my one finger," she said, and held it up high.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Up and down are opposites.
story:
Lucy ran into the playroom. Her big teddy sat on the small chair. "Today we slide!" said Lucy. She had a little slide right there, next to the doll bed.

Lucy climbed up, up, up the ladder. Then she zoomed down, fast. "Again!" she shouted. Her friend Ben came in. He held a warm cup of cocoa. "Mama made it," he said. "It was too hot, so we waited."

"Watch me!" said Lucy. She went up slow. Then she went down fast. Her arms opened wide. "Look, Ben!" Ben laughed and clapped. He put his cup on the shelf, far from the slide.

Lucy went up again. But her foot hit the cup handle. Oh no! The cocoa began to spill. Mama ran in fast. She grabbed the cup. "All safe," said Mama. Lucy climbed up the ladder one more time. Down, down, down she went. "Up and down!" she sang.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
knowledge_domain: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
fact: Grabbing a toy out of someone's hands can make them feel sad or angry.
story:
Adam was at the playground. He saw a big red truck. A boy named Sam was pushing it. Adam wanted the truck very much.

Adam grabbed the truck out of Sam's hands. Sam's face got red. Sam started to cry. Big tears ran down his cheeks. Adam looked at Sam. Sam did not push the truck anymore. He just cried and cried.

Adam gave the truck back. "Truck?" he asked. "My turn, please?" Sam wiped his tears. He nodded his head. "Okay. Wait for your turn," said Sam. Adam sat on the bench. He watched Sam push the truck down the slide ramp. It was noisy and fun to hear.

Then Sam ran back. "Your turn now," said Sam. Adam pushed the truck fast, fast, fast. "Thank you, Sam!" said Adam. Sam smiled. Then Sam asked, "My turn, please?" Adam gave the truck back. Now they took turns, over and over, until the sun went down.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Saying "sorry" is a way to show you know you hurt someone.
story:
Gabriel wanted to build a big tower. His friend Mia came over to play. Mia was building a tower too.

Gabriel ran to get more blocks. Oh no! His foot bumped Mia's tower. The blocks fell down. Crash!

Mia sat very still. Her lip went tight and small.

Gabriel looked at the blocks. He looked at Mia. What could he do?

"Sorry, Mia," Gabriel said.

Mia looked up. "Okay," she said. "Sorry is good."

Then Gabriel picked up a block. He put it at the bottom. "You build," he said. "Then me."

Mia stacked one block. Gabriel stacked one block. Then Mia. Then Gabriel.

"What color next?" asked Gabriel.

"Red," said Mia.

Gabriel found the red block. He gave it to her. She laughed. The tower grew so tall. It was taller than their teddy bear!

Then Daddy came in. He wiggled his fingers near Mia's toes. "Tickle, tickle!" he said.

Mia giggled. Gabriel giggled. The tower wobbled and fell down again.

"Uh oh!" said Gabriel. "Blocks again?"

"Yes, blocks again," said Mia.

They both picked up blocks together. This time the tower had two builders. It stood up straight and tall.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Flour is a dry powder that makes a little cloud when it is poured fast.
story:
Norah wants to make pancakes. She stands on her stool at the big counter. Dad holds the bowl.

"Can I pour the flour?" asks Norah.

"Yes," says Dad. "Pour it in."

Norah tips the cup fast. Whoosh! A big white cloud puffs up. The cloud lands on her nose. It lands on Dad's nose too. Norah looks at Dad. Dad looks like a snowman.

"You have a dusty nose," says Norah. She giggles.

"You have one too," says Dad. They laugh and laugh.

"Now I will pour slow," says Norah. She tips the cup little by little. No cloud. No dusty nose. The flour goes softly into the shiny bowl. Norah stirs the batter round and round.

Dad cooks the pancakes on the hot stove. Norah waits in her safe spot. Soon the pancakes come to the table.

Mama takes a bite. "Mmm," says Mama. "What is the name of the cook?"

"Norah!" says Norah. "The girl with the floury nose."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: A child's age is said with a number word, like 'I am four.'
story:
Iris sat at the dinner table. She wanted the big bowl of carrots. It was near Daddy.

Daddy held up one carrot. "One," said Iris. Daddy held up two carrots. "Two," said Iris.

Soon Iris had carrots on her plate. She counted them. "One, two, three, four." Then she ate one. "Now one, two, three," she said. Daddy smiled.

Mama set down the peas. "How many peas, Iris?" she asked.

Iris pointed at each pea. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight." Eight peas!

Then Grandma asked, "How old are you, Iris?"

Iris held up three little fingers. Then she said the number word out loud. "I am three!"

"Three!" said Grandma. "And next year you will be four."

The clock on the wall gave a little ring. Dinner time was over.

Iris put her three fingers near Grandma's plate. "One, two, three peas for you," she said, and pushed the bowl close.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Things can be sorted into groups, like animals, toys and foods.
story:
Penelope went to the store with Mama. She held the shopping list. "I can help," she said. "Yes, you can," said Mama.

Penelope dropped the picture basket by accident. It was on a low shelf. All the pictures fell out. Oh no! Apples, balls, cows, bread, ducks, teddy bears. What a mess!

"I will fix it," said Penelope. She made a pile of animals. Cow, duck, sheep. She made a pile of toys. Ball, teddy bear, drum. She made a pile of foods. Apple, bread, milk. Each pile had its own friends.

Mama came back. "Where did the mess go?" she asked. Penelope laughed. "It is not a mess now! Look, look, look!" She pointed at her three piles.

"You sorted them," said Mama. "Now help me shop. Find the foods we need." Penelope found the bread. She found the milk. She put them in the cart, one by one.

At home, Penelope made piles of her own toys. "Animals go here," she said. "Toys go there." Then she took her crayon. She drew a cow on the list. Mama laughed. "Is a cow a food?" she asked.

"No, Mama! A cow is an animal!" said Penelope. "Silly Mama." She kissed the cow picture good night.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Crayons can melt if they are left in a hot car on a sunny day.
story:
Charles wanted to draw a big sun. He went to get his crayons. But the crayon box was empty. Where did they go?

"Did you leave them somewhere?" Mom asked. Charles thought hard. Then he remembered. The crayons were in the car! He had taken them on the trip to Grandma's house. Charles and Mom went out to the car. The sun was bright and hot. The car felt hot too. Mom opened the door. Charles peeked inside. There was the box on the seat. He picked up a crayon. It felt soft. It bent like a worm! The orange one had gone flat and squishy.

"My crayons are bendy!" Charles said. Mom laughed. "Let's make something new," she said. She carried the box inside. Charles drew his sun with the bendy crayons. The soft tips made fat, smooth lines. It looked like the sun was glowing. "I like my sunny-day crayons," Charles said. He held one up to the window. It bent back and forth, back and forth.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: The hairdresser puts a cape around your shoulders to keep cut hair off your clothes.
story:
Elias sat in a big chair at the mall. His hair was long and it went in his eyes. "I want to see," said Elias. "A haircut will help," said Mom. A hairdresser named Joy came over.

Joy held up a soft cape. She put the cape around his shoulders. "Look, a superhero cape!" said Elias. He giggled and patted it. Joy began to snip. Little hairs fell down. They landed on the cape. They slid off his shirt and onto the floor.

Elias looked down. "The hairs did not get on me," he said. "No, the cape kept them off," said Joy. She brushed the hairs away. Then she turned the chair to the mirror. Elias saw his face. He could see! He smiled big. Mom took a photo. "New hair, happy boy," she said.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: You can pretend to take care of a doll or stuffed animal, like feeding it or tucking it into bed.
story:
Mohamed's teddy, Bruno, fell on the floor. "Are you sick, Bruno?" Mohamed asked. "Yes, I think you are."

Mohamed got his toy cup. He held it to Bruno's mouth. "Drink your medicine," he said. "Drink it all up." Bruno did not drink, but Mohamed pretended he did. "Good job, Bruno!"

Then Mohamed got a small blanket. He tucked Bruno into bed. "Sleep now," he said. "Sleep, sleep, sleep." He patted Bruno's soft head.

At lunch, Daddy made soup. It was hot, so Daddy blew on it. Mohamed watched. Then he blew on his toy cup too. "My soup is hot, Bruno," he said. "Wait for it."

After lunch, Mohamed looked at Bruno under the blanket. "Do you feel better?" he asked. He made a small voice. "I feel better."

Mohamed smiled. "Time for one more nap." He lay down next to Bruno. "Sleep, sleep, sleep," he whispered. And the room got very quiet.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Later means some time after now, not right away.
story:
Arnaud ran to the block corner at school. Tom was already there. Tom had all the blocks.

"Can I play too?" asked Arnaud.

"You can play later," said Tom. "Now I am making a robot."

Arnaud sat down on the small red chair. He looked at the clock. The big hand moved a tiny bit. Was it later now? He went back to Tom. "Is it later yet?" he asked.

"Not yet," said Tom. "My robot is not done."

Arnaud sat down again. He watched Tom stack the blocks. The robot got taller and taller. Where would its arms go? Then Tom picked up the loud drum from the toy shelf. He banged it twice. Boom, boom.

"That is my robot voice," said Tom.

Arnaud laughed. He found a box and began to fill it with crayons. He drew a robot with big square feet. He gave it red eyes and four wheels. The drawing took a long time. He colored the wheels and then the sky.

He looked up. Tom's tower was done. "Is it later now?" Arnaud asked.

Tom looked at the blocks. He looked at Arnaud's drawing. "Yes," said Tom. "It is later now."

They sat down together. Arnaud filled the robot's tummy with blocks. Tom made the loud drum go boom, boom, boom.

"Tomorrow," said Tom, "we can make a spaceship."

"Today is robots," said Arnaud. "Tomorrow is spaceships. And yesterday we made nothing at all."

Tom hit the drum one more time. "Boom," he said. "Robot says yes."

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Colors come in lighter and darker kinds, like light blue and dark blue, and both are still called blue.
story:
Evan sat in the backyard with his paint pots. His friend Mia came over with her crayons. Mia held up a dark blue crayon. "This is not blue," she said. "Blue is like the sky."

Evan looked up. The morning sky was light blue. He looked at his paint pot. That blue was dark. He dipped his brush and painted a big wet stripe on the paper. "Look," he said. "Dark blue." Mia dipped her crayon next to it. "Light blue," she said.

They lined up all the blues on the grass. Light blue, blue, dark blue. "They are all blue!" said Mia. Evan painted one more stripe. It was a polite little stripe, small and neat, just for Mia. The paint smelled like rain. A bee buzzed by the yellow flowers, and Mia laughed.

"Red next?" asked Evan. He held up the red pot.

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: A book's title is its name.
story:
Colton wanted his favorite book at bedtime. It was the book about the duck. But the shelf was full of books, and he could not find it.

Colton pulled out a book. He opened the front cover. He looked at the first page. This book had a bear in it. Not the duck book. He put it back. He took out another one. He opened it slowly, front cover first. That one had a truck. Not the duck book either.

"Colton, it is bedtime soon," said Dad from the hallway. Colton kept looking. His tummy felt a little jumpy. He wanted the duck book so much.

Then he saw the big words on the front of a book. The words said "Little Duck." Dad had pointed to them one night. Colton ran his smooth finger under the letters. He opened the front cover. Page by page, the duck swam. The duck made its boat float on the pond.

Colton climbed into bed with the book. He turned each page, one at a time. Dad sat down beside him. "Read it," said Colton. Dad started at the front. "Little Duck," he read, "went out one morning."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Christmas, many families decorate a tree.
story:
Sarah went to the big hall with her family. The hall had a Christmas tree. It was tall and green. Sarah wanted to hang the ornaments all by herself.

She put a red ball on one branch. Then she put a star there too. Then a little wooden boat. Soon one branch was full. The branch bent down low. "Oh no," said Sarah. "The branch is too heavy."

Grandma came to help. "Try another branch," said Grandma. Sarah hung the red ball up high. She hung the star on the other side. The soft little boat went on a low branch. She counted them: one, two, three. Now the ornaments were all around the tree. The branches stood up tall again.

The tree looked pretty from every side. Sarah smiled and hung one more star, way up high, where everyone could see it.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Adding white paint to a color makes it lighter, so red with white becomes pink.
story:
Kinsley sat on the playroom floor. She wanted to make a card for Grandma. The card needed a pink flower on it. She looked in her paint box. She found red paint. She found blue paint. She found yellow paint. She found green paint. But there was no pink paint.

Kinsley made the grass first. She painted green grass at the bottom. She painted a yellow sun up high. Then she tried to paint the flower. She dipped her brush in the red paint. She made a red flower. She shook her head. "Grandma wants pink," she said.

Then she saw the white paint jar. She put red paint in a cup. She added a little white paint. She stirred it round and round. She heard a swishy sound. The paint turned pink! Kinsley clapped her hands. She painted a big pink flower.

Then Kinsley washed her brush in the water. The water turned pink too. She laughed. She painted three small pink flowers next to the big one. Mom came in to look. "A pink flower for me?" said Grandma's voice from the door. Kinsley held up the card and ran to her.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: An indoor cat uses a litter box as its toilet.
story:
Norah came home with a small cat. The cat was gray and soft. Norah hugged her teddy bear tight. "Where will the cat sleep?" she asked. "In this soft bed," said Dad.

Then Norah had a worry. "Where does the cat go potty?" Dad set a box on the floor. It was full of sand. Norah poured a little more sand in. The cat sniffed the box. The cat stepped in. The cat dug a small hole.

Norah waited. The cat used the box! Then the cat covered the hole with sand. "Wow," said Norah. "That is so smart." Dad smiled. "You are smart too," he said. "You helped make the cat's potty." Norah patted the cat's head. The cat purred like a tiny motor.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Everybody has feelings, even grown-ups.
story:
Weston ran to the playground with Dad. He saw the tall slide. His tummy felt funny. "I am scared," he said. The slide looked so big.

Dad sat on the bench. "I was scared of slides too," said Dad. Weston stopped. He looked at Dad. Dad was big. Dad was tall. Dad had been scared? Weston thought about that. Grown-ups had feelings too!

Weston held Dad's hand. He walked to the slide. He touched it with one finger. It was cool and smooth. Dad stood close by. Weston climbed one step. Then two steps. His heart went fast, but it felt like happy-fast now.

Down he went! Whee! He laughed and laughed. "I did it!" he said. He was so excited. Then he saw a little girl crying by the swing. Her ice cream had fallen. Weston felt sad for her. Dad had a napkin. He wiped her hands. She smiled.

Then a small dog ran by with a red hat in its mouth. The dog dropped the hat right on Weston's head. Weston laughed again. Dad laughed too. "Home time," said Dad, and Weston held his hand all the way.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: Cutting a square from one corner to the opposite corner makes two triangles.
story:
Juliette sat at the art table. She wanted to make a paper sailboat. She had a brown square of paper. She also had a long rectangle for the boat.

But a sailboat needs a sail. Juliette looked and looked. She needed two triangles. She had no triangles at all.

Miss Amy came over. "Hold your square still," she said. She took the scissors. "Scissors are for grown-ups." She cut from one corner to the opposite corner. Then Juliette saw them. Two triangles! The square had made two triangles.

Juliette tapped the triangles on the table. Tap, tap. She glued one triangle on top of the rectangle. The sail stood up tall.

Then she drew a tree on green paper. She added a brown root going down into the dirt. "Don't taste the glue," said Miss Amy. "I won't," said Juliette.

She put her sailboat in her cubby. She could not wait to show Mama. "Look at my sail," she whispered to the boat.

activity: getting a first haircut at a salon
knowledge_domain: getting a first haircut at a salon
fact: A hairdresser uses a comb to keep hair neat while cutting it.
story:
Zoey sat in the big salon chair. Her feet did not touch the floor. Today she would get her first haircut.

The hairdresser was named Mia. Mia had a silver comb and small scissors. Zoey was scared of the scissors. "They look pointy," she said.

Mia smiled. "Just watch what I do first," she said. She combed a piece of Zoey's hair. Comb, comb, comb. Then one little snip. Zoey counted on her fingers. "Three combs, then a snip!" she said.

Mia did it again. Comb, comb, comb. Snip. Zoey counted every time. The counting made her forget to be scared.

Then Zoey saw something. The comb made her hair flat and tidy before each snip. The snipped hair fell in neat little pieces, not big messy ones. They slid down like soft rain.

"Your hair is very neat," Zoey said.

"You helped," said Mia. "You kept counting for me."

At dinner that night, Zoey ate a lemon and made a sour face. Then she smiled. "Three combs, then a snip," she said, and she combed her doll's hair with her fingers.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: During Hanukkah, Jewish families light candles on a menorah for eight nights.
story:
Oliver went to the big cultural center with his mom and his grandma. Today was Hanukkah. The room smelled like pancakes and apples. There were pretty blue and gold flags on the walls.

A tall man stood by a menorah. It had holders for eight candles, plus one more candle in the middle. Oliver wanted to help. "Can I light one?" he asked.

"Grown-ups light the candles," said the man kindly. "But you can count with me." The man used the middle candle to light two little candles. They popped and glowed. Oliver counted out loud. "One, two!" The flames made warm light on his face.

"You know what my secret job is?" said the man. "I come back every night. And each night, we light one more candle." Oliver's eyes got big. "So tomorrow there will be three?" he asked. "And then four?"

"Yes," said the man. "All the way to eight." Oliver held his grandma's hand tight. "Can we come back tomorrow?" he asked. "I want to count again." His grandma smiled. "We will come back," she said. Oliver waved to the little flames. "See you tomorrow, candles."

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: A day goes from morning, to afternoon, to evening, to night.
story:
Violet got to daycare in the morning. The sun was low and small. She hung her coat on her little hook. Her friend Ben was already there. They built a tall tower in the block corner.

After lunch, the class lay down for a nap. Violet slept for a long time. When she woke up, she rubbed her eyes. The light in the room was big and gold. "It is morning," said Violet. "Time for breakfast."

Miss Ana smiled. "Look out the window," she said. The sun was high and bright. "It is not morning now. It is afternoon."

Violet looked out. The sun had moved. It was not where it was before. The day had gone on and on, past morning, all the way to afternoon.

"Now we have a cold snack," said Miss Ana. She poured milk into little cups. Violet drank hers slowly. The milk was cold and good.

"After snack we play outside," said Miss Ana. "Later, your mommy comes."

Violet played in the sand. Then the door opened. Mommy stood there with her big bag.

"Mommy! It is afternoon now," said Violet. "And now it is going home time."

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Setting the cup down on the table before pouring keeps it still.
story:
Aubrey wanted to do it all by herself. Daddy had made the toast, and now it sat on her plate. "Can I put on the butter?" she asked. "Yes, you may," said Daddy. Aubrey picked up the little knife. Daddy held it with her, and they spread the soft butter together. The toast turned shiny and gold.

Next came the milk. Aubrey held her cup in one hand. She tried to pour with the other hand. The cup wiggled. The milk made a puddle on the table. "Oops," said Aubrey. She set the cup down on the table first. Then she poured. The cup sat still. The milk went right in, all the way to the top. Not one drop spilled.

"Look what I can do!" said Aubrey. Daddy clapped. Aubrey took a big bite of her buttery toast. Then she drank her milk, sip by sip.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Toast is bread that has been heated until it turns brown and crunchy.
story: Felix put his itchy sweater sleeve up high, out of the way. Mom put two soft white slices into the toaster. Felix waited and counted. "One, two, three," he said. Pop! The slices jumped up. Felix looked and looked. The bread was not white now. It was brown. It crunched when Mom tapped it. "The toaster made it brown and crunchy," he whispered. Mom set the toast on his plate. Felix took the butter knife. He spread, spread, spread, slow and smooth. The butter went soft and melty. Then he held the milk jug with two hands. He poured, a little, a little more. Not one drop spilled. He drank it all and smiled. "Again tomorrow," said Felix. Mom laughed. "We can buy more bread, and you can spread again."

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: Mixing red paint and yellow paint makes orange paint.
story:
Evan sat at the paint table. He wanted to paint a pumpkin. But there was no orange paint.

Evan looked at the cups. Red paint. Blue paint. Yellow paint. Green paint. No orange at all. He frowned at his paper.

His friend Mia came over. "I know a trick," she said. She put red paint on the brush. Then she added yellow paint. "Now stir it," she said.

Evan stirred slow, then fast. The paint turned orange! "It looks neat!" said Evan. He hurried to paint his pumpkin.

Mia made a green leaf for the top. Then she looked at her paper. "I want purple," she said.

Evan smiled. "Try the trick," he said. Mia stirred blue and red. It turned purple! "Whoa," said Mia.

Their teacher hung both pictures on the wall. Evan pointed at his pumpkin. "Orange is red and yellow," he told her. "I made it myself."

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: Many Muslims say 'Bismillah,' which means 'in the name of God,' before they eat.
story:
Ruby was at Nana's house. Her tummy was rumbling like a tiny drum. Nana put rice and peas on the table. "Yum!" said Ruby. She picked up her spoon, fast.

Nana held up her hand. "Wait, little one," she said. "We say Bismillah first." Ruby put her spoon down. It went clink on the plate. "Bismillah," Ruby tried. It felt fuzzy in her mouth, like a new sock on the wrong foot. Nana laughed a kind laugh. "Almost! Say it with me."

"Bismillah," they said together. Then Ruby took a big bite. The peas were sweet. Later, after her nap, they would drive to the park. But first, one more bite. "Bismillah," said Ruby, all by herself. Nana clapped her hands.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: Feeling nervous on the first day of school is okay.
story:
Mason stepped onto the big school bus. He held his dad's hand tight. The doors closed with a soft whoosh. Mason sat by the tall glass window.

His tummy felt funny. It felt like little butterflies were in there. Mason looked down at his shoes. He did not say a word.

A boy sat down next to him. The boy had a blue backpack. The boy looked down at his shoes too. Mason tapped the glass with one finger. Tap, tap. The boy looked up. Mason smiled at him. Then the boy smiled back. Mason's tummy felt a little better.

Dad sat across the aisle. He leaned over softly. "My tummy felt funny on my first day too," Dad said. "I was nervous then. It was okay." Mason nodded. He looked out the window again.

The bus stopped by the school. Mason picked up his small backpack. He waved to the boy with the blue backpack. The boy waved back. They walked to the classroom door together. Mason put his hand on the door. He took one big breath. The butterflies flew away, little by little. He pushed the door open, and the room was full of toys.

"Look," said the boy. "Blocks!" Mason ran to see.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: An apron or an old shirt keeps paint off your clothes.
story:
Amelia ran to the art room. She wore her new blue shirt today. She wanted to paint a big cat.

Teacher Sam held up a red paint pot. "This is red," said Amelia. Then she pointed to the yellow pot. "And that is yellow!" Teacher Sam smiled.

Amelia reached for a brush. Then she stopped. Paint could drip. Paint could splash. Her new shirt was her favorite shirt. She grabbed the big apron from the hook. She put it on all by herself. "Now my shirt is safe," she said.

She scooped red paint. She scooped yellow paint. She mixed them in her tray. The paint turned orange! Amelia clapped. Orange like a pumpkin. Orange like a fox.

She painted a big orange cat. One little drop fell on her apron. Amelia looked down at her shirt. Still clean and blue!

"Look, Teacher Sam!" she called, holding up her work. "My cat is orange and my shirt is still blue!"

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: In English, we write from left to right across the page.
story:
Ryan sat at the little desk in the library. He had a red pencil and some paper. He wanted to write his name all by himself.

He gripped the pencil in his fist. The letters came out wobbly. He tried again with two fingers, like the librarian showed him. That felt better.

Ryan started his R at the right side of the paper. He wrote A, then Y. Uh oh. There was no room left. The N fell off the edge of the page. Ryan made a sour face. "My name does not fit," he said.

He thought for a minute. He looked at the book next to him. The words started at the left side of the page.

Ryan got a new sheet. He started the R on the left this time. A, then Y, then A, then N. They all fit.

The librarian leaned over the desk. "Ryan," she read out loud. She drew a little star next to it. Ryan smiled and traced the letters one more time.

activity: spending a surprise snow day at home
knowledge_domain: spending a surprise snow day at home
fact: Feet leave footprints in fresh snow.
story: Grayson looked out the window. Snow was falling on the grass. "No school today!" said Mom. Grayson clapped his hands. He wanted to find his toy plane. It was lost somewhere outside. He had left it after playing yesterday. Grayson put on his boots. Mom came outside with him. The snow was fresh and bumpy. Then Grayson saw marks on the ground. They looked like little holes in a row. "Look, Mom! What is that?" he asked. "Follow them and see," said Mom. Grayson stepped in the snow. His boots made marks too. His marks looked just like the other marks. He followed them step by step. The marks went past the big tree. They went up to the neighbor's door. There sat his red plane, safe on the step. Grayson laughed. "My feet made marks too, Mom!" They walked home side by side, two trails of footprints behind them, and the plane tucked under his arm.

activity: starting the first day of school
knowledge_domain: starting the first day of school
fact: A backpack is a bag you carry on your back.
story:
Felix stood at the gate of the school playground. His new backpack sat on his back. It was very heavy. He could not walk fast. He wanted to run to the slide, but his feet went slow, slow, slow.

A girl named Mia ran past him. She looked at his big backpack. "Why is it so big?" she asked. Felix sat down on the wooden bench. He opened his backpack. Out came a toy bear. Out came a toy truck. Out came three picture books. The backpack got lighter. Felix put his toys in a safe pile.

Now his backpack was small and light on his back. Felix stood up. He ran to the slide with Mia. His feet went fast, fast, fast. He went down the slide and laughed. "I will remember," said Felix. "A backpack is for carrying, not for toys." Mia held his toy bear, and they went to play again.

activity: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
knowledge_domain: to clap along to the steady beat of a song and sing a nursery rhyme from memory
fact: A song can be played or sung fast or slow.
story:
Isabella wanted to sing the whole rhyme by herself. Miss Rosa had a shiny drum and a big smile. "Sing with me," said Miss Rosa. "One, two, three, clap!"

They sang very fast. "Hickory dickory dock, the mouse ran up the clock!" Isabella's words got all tangled. She said "hickory hickory dockery" and laughed. The words fell over like blocks.

Miss Rosa tapped the drum slowly. Booom. Booom. "Let's try it slow," she said. Isabella clapped with each slow tap. Her hands went clap, clap, clap. She sang, "Hickory... dickory... dock." The words came out just right. The mouse ran up the clock. The clock struck one. The mouse ran down. Then Isabella sang about a cat with a long tail. "Pussy cat, pussy cat, where have you been?"

Then Miss Rosa tapped the drum fast. Isabella sang the fast song too. Her feet jumped. Her pigtails flew up.

"I did it!" said Isabella. "Fast mouse. Slow mouse. I can do both!"

Miss Rosa tapped the drum one more time. Booom. Booom.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: Tablets are kept away from water and drinks.
story:
Zachary sat in the school computer lab. His teacher, Miss Ana, put a tablet on the table. "I want to draw," Zachary said. "But I don't know how."

"Press the round button," said Miss Ana. Zachary pressed it. The screen lit up. His eyes went wide. He tapped a green icon. The drawing app opened. "I did it!" he said.

Miss Ana gave him a cup of juice. He set it down next to the tablet. Miss Ana shook her head. She moved the cup to the far table. Zachary watched her. Then he nodded and kept drawing.

He drew a blue pond. He drew a yellow duck on the pond. "That's for you," he told Miss Ana. "I like it," she said.

At last it was time to go. Zachary pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He carried the tablet with two careful hands. He put it back on the shelf, all by himself.

"Can we sell my duck picture at the school fair?" he asked. Miss Ana laughed. "Let's print it first," she said. She held his hand and they walked out together.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: After a visit ends, families can stay in touch with phone calls, video calls or letters.
story:
Grandma came to sleep in the guest bedroom. Elizabeth helped make the bed. She tucked the blanket in tight. "One pillow for you," she said. "One pillow for Ted the bear." Grandma laughed and put Ted by the window, where a bird was building a nest.

Each day they did things together. One, they baked bread. Two, they picked peas. Three, they read books in the guest room. Elizabeth loved having Grandma there.

Then the week was over. Grandma put her bag by the door. Elizabeth felt wobbly and sad. "Draw me a picture," said Grandma. "Put it in a letter. I will write back." So Elizabeth drew the bird's nest and the blue eggs. Mom helped her mail it. On Friday the phone rang. Grandma's voice said, "Your picture is on my wall!" Elizabeth ran to get her crayons.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn.
story:
Jasmine ran to the door with her shiny red boots. "Can we go to the park?" she asked. "It is sunny today!"

"First we stop for sunscreen," said Mom. "Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn."

Jasmine stood still. Mom put white cream on her face, her arms, and her neck. Then they took the long walk to the park.

At the park, the wind blew. The wind made the leaves dance. "Why do the leaves move?" Jasmine asked. "The windy day pushes them," said Mom.

Jasmine looked up at the big sky. No clouds came. The sun stayed out all day. Her friend Ben came with a rain hat, but it was not rainy. "Take it off," Jasmine said, and Ben laughed.

When they got home, Jasmine looked in the mirror. Her skin was not red at all. She clapped her hands and said, "Sunscreen, sunny day, we can go again tomorrow!"

activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: Some languages, like Arabic and Hebrew, are read from right to left.
story:
Mohamed wanted his bedtime story. But where was his book?

"Here it is," said Papa. "Yossi gave you this one at daycare."

The book looked funny. It opened from the other side. Mohamed turned it over and over. Which way did it go?

He opened the front cover. The words were all at the wrong end! He flipped the book. Now the words sat at the start. "It goes this way," he said.

The story was about a little turtle. The turtle ate leaves. Then the turtle began to grow. It grew and grew.

Mohamed pointed at the marks on the page. "What are these?" he asked.

"Those are the words," said Papa. "They tell the story."

Mohamed traced the letters with his finger. The letters made words. The words made the turtle! He turned one page, then another. Each page had more story.

The turtle spun in a circle and felt dizzy. Mohamed laughed.

"One more page?" he asked.

Papa turned the page.

activity: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
knowledge_domain: weather words such as sunny, rainy, windy and snowy and the clothes that go with them
fact: On a rainy day, a raincoat helps keep your body dry.
story:
Samuel wanted to build a sand castle in the backyard. It was a sunny morning. He wore his sun hat. Then the sky turned gray. Big clouds came. The wind blew. Samuel's hat flew off. He ran to catch it.

"Rain is coming," said Mama. Samuel ran outside without his coat. The rain came down. His hair got wet. His shirt got wet too. He ran back inside.

Samuel put on his red raincoat. He put on his rain boots. Then he went back out. The rain fell on the raincoat. It ran down the sleeves. His body stayed dry. He looked under the coat. "Dry!" said Samuel. He stomped in a quiet little puddle. The rain went drip, drip, drip. Samuel built his castle in the wet sand.

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A rectangle has four sides and four square corners, like the shape of a door.
story:
Naomi wanted to win the shape game. "Find a rectangle," said Mom. Naomi looked around the playroom. Her round ball was not it. Her square block had four sides, all the same. That was not it either. Her triangle flag had pointy corners. Not it.

"I am thirsty," said Naomi. She walked to the door to get her cup. She stopped. She looked at the door. It was tall and flat. She put one finger on a corner. "One, two, three, four," she counted. Four corners. She ran her finger down each side. Four sides.

"Mom! The door is a rectangle!"

"You win the game," said Mom.

At snack time, Naomi pointed her fork at her toast. "That is a rectangle too," she said. She took a big bite.
